title: The guest house
hookLine: a new arrival each morning, joy or grief or meanness, and each to be welcomed (Masnavi 5.3644ff)

lines: AS IF THE MOOD OWNED THE HOUSE.
cards: You wake up, and before your feet touch the floor, something's already there. A heaviness, for no reason. Or a buzzy excitement.
Or a low irritation that'll follow you to the coffee machine. You didn't invite it. It just arrived in the night.
It's easy to treat these moods as who we are. I'm anxious. I'm a grump today.
As if the mood owned the house. Rumi had another way to see it, in a passage a modern poem was later built on. Today, back to what Rumi himself wrote.

teach.b: It's in Book Five of the Masnavi. Every day, Rumi says, at every moment, a different thought comes into your heart like an honored guest.
Treat each thought as a person, he says, because a person's worth comes from their thoughts and their soul. Then the surprising part.
If a sad thought arrives and seems to be chasing away your joy, it may be making room for joy.
It sweeps the house clear, he says, so that new joy, from the source of all good, can come in.

It shakes the yellow leaves off the branch of the heart, so fresh green leaves can grow. It pulls up the old roots of happiness, so new ones can come from beyond. So be welcoming, Rumi says, even to the sorrow.
Don't slam the door. You don't know what it's bringing. That modern poem opens by calling a human being a guest house.
It's a modern rendering, still under copyright, so I'm staying close to Rumi's own lines here. Both share the core picture. You're the house, and the moods are guests.
A guest comes, stays a while, and leaves.
A guest isn't the owner. That changes how you meet a hard morning. Not: I am anxious.
But: anxiety is visiting. Offer it a chair, and see what it came to say. It will not stay forever.
No guest does. Your line: a guest, not the owner.

how: Readers of Rumi, and some meditation teachers, use this picture of moods as guests, naming what arrives and letting it stay and leave, rather than taking it as who they are.

o: a stranger to keep politely at arm's length
a friend who has overstayed their welcome
a passing mood or thought to welcome, not obey

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: sweeps the house clear for joy
shaken off so green ones can grow
you, with the moods as guests

s: the well-known 'guest house' poem is Rumi's own wording
it's a modern rendering, still under copyright. Rumi's lines are in Book Five of the Masnavi.
Rumi says even sorrow may be making room for joy
it sweeps the house clear so new joy can come in.
Rumi says to shut the door on sad thoughts
he says welcome them. you don't know what they're bringing.

games.q: you wake up and a heavy sadness is already there. what does Rumi's guest house suggest?
o: decide this is who you are now.
welcome it as a guest; it may be clearing room for joy.
slam the door and keep busy.
games.why: Rumi says treat each thought as an honored guest. sorrow may be sweeping the house clean for new joy.

practice: Ask: who's visiting right now? Maybe tiredness, maybe hope, maybe a little worry; give it a simple name and greet it inside, the way you'd greet someone at the door: oh, hello, worry, come in.
Let it sit with you, and notice it isn't you; it's only staying for a while.

wordCard.voice: Guest. Rumi says every thought and mood comes into the heart like a guest, and even sorrow may be clearing room for joy. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a guest. Rumi's word for each thought that comes into the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: a guest, not the owner. You're the house. That's day two hundred fourteen.
